Both `bun run typecheck` and `bun test` pass cleanly.

## Summary

The bug was in `PostController.update()` (`app/Http/Controllers/PostController.ts`), which built its success response by hand as `new Response(null, { status: 302, headers: { Location: ... } })` instead of using the framework's `this.redirect()` helper that `store()` and `destroy()` already use. That helper auto-selects status 303 for any non-GET request, which is required here: when Inertia/the browser follows a redirect issued in response to a PUT, it re-sends the *same* method (PUT) unless the server responds 303 (which forces the follow-up to be a GET). Because `update()` hardcoded 302, the successful save's redirect caused the browser to PUT `/posts/<id>` again, hitting `update()` again, looping forever into `net::ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` — even though the edit had already been saved on the first request. The fix replaces the raw `Response` with `return this.redirect(\`/posts/${post.id}\`)`, matching the working `store`/`destroy` actions and producing a 303 that safely downgrades the follow-up to GET.

I also added a regression test in `tests/PostController.test.ts` (`posts.update` describe block) that creates a user and post directly via the ORM, signs in via `TestApp.actingAs()` + `withCsrf()`, PUTs an edit, and asserts the response is `303` with `Location: /posts/<id>` — this would have failed against the old 302 code path.
